<reason>CON built the more decisive comparative frame (money is fungible, so universal free meals for well-off families necessarily compete with quality/summer/breakfast dollars for poor kids) and used the Pressure Questions round most effectively: its Q2 forced PRO to either ring-fence anti-poverty spending or concede the tradeoff, and PRO's answer ("budgets aren't infinite... a legislative choice") was a real concession that CON exploited through the rest of the debate. CON also neutralized PRO's stigma pillar by noting cashless serving lines already erase visible sorting without going universal, and PRO never squarely answered why universalism adds anything beyond that technological fix. CON's "regressive squeezing" reframe (a thinner universal tray costs the poor child everything and the rich child nothing) directly undercut PRO's closing "squeezed vs. eliminated" durability argument, and PRO's final speech never engaged with it, instead repeating the same asymmetry claim. PRO kept a genuinely live point on cliff-edges (moving the eligibility line relocates rather than eliminates the edge), which CON only partially answered via phase-out tiers, and PRO's history-based durability claim about targeted programs being cut outright also remained live and ungutted. But on balance CON did more of the decisive comparative work and closed the debate more cleanly. CON is penalized somewhat for having a rebuttal turn clipped for exceeding the word limit, which is a real execution cost, keeping the margin from being larger.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Pressure Question on ring-fencing summer feeding/breakfast/food quality, followed by PRO's hedged non-answer ("budgets aren't infinite... a legislative choice"), which CON then converted into the closing's central indictment of universalism as an unfunded promise paid for by the neediest.</best_rebuttal>
